text.p: Swissair Cargo and Logistics, which will become an independent division in the Swissair Group on January 1, 1997, is expected to be profitable in 1996 despite a generally weak year, said Klaus Knappik, head of the new division.
But expectations have been curbed due to the unexpectedly weak business, a new development in the air cargo business, Knappik said in Swissair's internal magazine, Swissair News.
"I expect a positive result for Swissair Cargo," Knappik said in response to a question from the magazine on the business performance at air cargo.

Swissair has not reported divisional results in the past, but its cargo division was profitable in 1995, a spokesman confirmed. The adoption of International Accounting Standards (IAS), however, means divisional profits will be reported.
Weak business conditions this year contrast with past years, when cargo business grew continously. Over the last 12 months or so, business has stagnated and declined in some markets.
Knappik said this shocked some suppliers who reacted by cutting prices eventhough cargo is not faced with the same excess capacity as the passenger business.
All the necessary steps required for turning Cargo & Logistics into a separate unit have been taken, but the only thing missing is a transformation of the mind and approach of employees.
Such a mental shift means that employees identify with their own unit and raise their involvement in business, Knappik said.
Like Swissair's passenger business, cargo is also fighting with yield erosion, an issue that concerns Knappik.
However, he said that the air cargo business continues to expand and one must get used to a situation of bad years following good years.
"In the future the market will feel the effects of economic fluctuations much more than in the past," Knappik said.
Knappik's response to the tougher environment is to emphasise quality consistently.
"The Wild West times in air cargo, where anyone could make money more or less quickly, are over," Knappick said.
